expectations.text: Does NOT approve the handoff as-is
expectations.evidence: "Not yet — hold it before handing off to the migration owner."

expectations.text: Flags the 367-of-511 concentration in a single file as anomalous or suspicious
expectations.evidence: "367 of 511 call sites (72%) sitting in a single file is the kind of result that's either a genuine hotspot... or a sign the count is wrong"

expectations.text: Asks what the top file actually is, or asks to see the file list, before accepting
expectations.evidence: Step 1: "Spot-check the top file independently — e.g. grep -c for the actual pattern census used, read a sample of the matched lines, confirm they're real call sites" — requires identifying/opening the top file before accepting the number.

expectations.text: Distinguishes schema validity from substantive correctness
expectations.evidence: "JSON validity, presence of the 4 required keys, and exactly 10 entries... are all *format* checks... they say nothing about whether the counts inside that schema are correct. 'Validates' is not the same claim as 'accurate.'"

expectations.text: Proposes an independent re-count or other ground-truth check rather than trusting the reported number
expectations.evidence: "Cross-check the total (511) against one independent method (different grep pattern, or an IDE/LSP 'find references' if available)."

expectations.text: Raises the possibility that matches came from data/config/fixtures rather than executable code
expectations.evidence: Only raises code-side false-positive causes — "a regex that also caught comments/strings/imports" and "comments/log strings/dead code" — never floats that the top file itself could be a non-code data/config/fixture file (vs. a real source hotspot). 'Generated file' and 'vendored copy' are the closest terms but describe generated/copied CODE, not a data manifest listing violations as data. No explicit data/config/fixture hypothesis — vaguely adjacent only.
